title: Your vow
hookLine: a vow in your own words for the years ahead
tomorrow: a man with a terrible past must say one true sentence. which one?

cards: A coach says you've made the team; a manager offers the promotion. The win is right there. The young seeker in the Majjhima Nikaya turned one down, twice.
He studies with Alara Kalama and reaches the same meditation his teacher reached. Alara offers to lead the community with him, as equals. He says no and walks away.
Then he studies with Uddaka Ramaputta, reaches that height too, and is offered the place of teacher. He walks away again. What wasn't enough?
The sutta says it plainly: those states didn't lead to awakening, to peace, to the end of suffering.

teach.b: In another sutta, the Buddha names two things he learned along the way: not to settle for good states, and not to shrink back while striving. Then he gives the resolve he made, and he says it in the body.
Let only skin and sinew and bone remain, let the flesh and blood dry up; I will not stop until I reach what human strength can reach.
That's a vow you can feel: the skin of your hands, the cords at your wrists, the bones you're sitting on right now.
Buddhists have a word for this: adhitthana, resolve, a vow set down like a foundation stone. Theravada lists it among the perfections, the qualities a Buddha-to-be grows over lifetimes.
In Zen halls, the bodhisattva vows are chanted after sitting: beings are numberless, I vow to free them. The words differ from school to school. The shape is the same.
A vow isn't a wish. It's where you stand when the good-enough offer arrives.

teach.h: IN YOUR OWN WORDS, BY HAND.
teach.b: Year five is near its summit, and this block asks for one thing: a vow in your own words, for the years ahead.
Not the Buddha's words. Yours. Small enough to keep, and set down by hand, like a stone.

how: Buddhists make resolves at many scales: Theravada practitioners speak of adhitthana as a perfection, and in Zen and other Mahayana communities the bodhisattva vows are chanted together, often at the end of a sitting.

o: a promise to a teacher that you'll obey him
a wish you write down and hope comes true
a resolve in your own words for the years ahead

games.q: the vow, from the seeker's own story — tap the pairs.
p: offered to lead with him as equals
offered him the place of teacher
resolve, set like a foundation stone
the body the resolve is spoken in

s: the Buddha's first teachers taught him nothing at all
he reached what each of them had reached; it just didn't lead to awakening.
a vow is basically a strong wish about the future
adhitthana is resolve: where you stand when the good-enough offer arrives.
the Buddha described his resolve in terms of skin, sinew and bone
let only skin, sinew and bone remain; he would not stop short.

games.q: you're offered captain of the debate team, but you'd set that time aside for the portfolio you promised yourself you'd finish. what does the seeker's story point to?
o: take captain; a good offer is a sign to change course.
measure the offer against the vow; good isn't the same as what you set out for.
do both halfway, so nobody is disappointed.
games.why: the seeker turned down two good offers because they didn't lead where he'd set out to go. a vow is what you measure the offers against.

practice: Take a pen and paper, and feel the pen's weight and the paper under the side of your hand. Write one sentence that begins I vow, for the years ahead, small enough to keep.
Then put the pen down, rest both hands flat on the page, and feel the bones of your hands while the sit runs.

wordCard.voice: Your vow: adhitthana, resolve, the foundation stone you stand on when good enough comes calling.

orig.note: Pali: resolve, determination; in Theravada lists, one of the perfections.

carryVoice: Keep this: my vow, in my own words, by my own hand. Forty-three days into the block.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 26 (Ariyapariyesana Sutta: leaving Alara Kalama and Uddaka Ramaputta)
Anguttara Nikaya 2.5 (not settling for wholesome states; the skin, sinew and bone resolve)
The four great bodhisattva vows (chanted in Zen communities, traced to Zhiyi)
